1 Thessalonians 1.audience: Gentile believers who had turned from the gods of their city and had suffered for it would have heard that their faith was known across Macedonia and Achaia.

culture.title: Thessalonica
culture.text: Thessalonica was the capital of the province of Macedonia and a free city on the Via Egnatia, the main Roman road across the Balkans.

culture.title: Turned from idols
culture.text: Most of the believers were Gentiles who had worshiped the city's gods. Thessalonica had temples to Serapis, Dionysus, and the Cabiri, and honored Rome and the emperor.

1 Thessalonians 2.audience: Paul reminds the church how he, Silvanus, and Timothy behaved among them after being "shamefully entreated" at Philippi (1 Thessalonians 2:2).

culture.title: Wandering teachers
culture.text: Traveling philosophers and religious teachers were common, and many were accused of flattery and greed.

culture.title: As a nurse
culture.text: Wealthier families hired a wet nurse to feed and raise their children.

culture.title: Labouring night and day
culture.text: Paul supported himself by working with his hands, probably at tentmaking (Acts 18:3).

1 Thessalonians 3.audience: Young believers under pressure, who may have feared that Paul had forgotten them, would have heard of his longing to see them and his prayer that they grow in love.

culture.title: Left at Athens alone
culture.text: Paul had been sent from Berea to Athens for his safety, while Silas and Timothy stayed behind (Acts 17:13–15).

culture.title: Afflictions
culture.text: In Thessalonica a mob dragged Jason before the city rulers because he had hosted Paul (Acts 17:5–9).

1 Thessalonians 4.audience: Paul writes about sexual purity, quiet work, and believers who have died, so that the living "sorrow not, even as others which have no hope" (1 Thessalonians 4:13).

culture.title: Possessing his vessel
culture.text: "Vessel" may mean one's own body or one's wife; translators differ.

culture.title: Grief without hope
culture.text: Greek and Roman tombstones often express hopelessness; one common formula said that the dead person once was not, then was, and now is not and cares not.

culture.title: To meet the Lord
culture.text: The Greek word for "meet" was used for citizens going out of a city to welcome an arriving dignitary (Acts 28:15).

1 Thessalonians 5.audience: Believers worried about the day of the Lord would have heard that they were children of light, not appointed to wrath, and received short commands for daily life together.

culture.title: Peace and safety
culture.text: Roman coins and inscriptions celebrated the peace (pax) and security (securitas) of Roman rule.

culture.title: As a thief in the night
culture.text: Jesus used the same image (Matthew 24:43; Luke 12:39).

culture.title: Breastplate and helmet
culture.text: Paul borrows from Isaiah 59:17, where God puts on righteousness as a breastplate and "an helmet of salvation upon his head."

2 Thessalonians 1.audience: Persecuted believers would have heard that their endurance was a token of the righteous judgment of God and that rest would come when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven.

culture.title: Flaming fire
culture.text: Fire accompanies God's appearing in the Old Testament (Exodus 3:2; Isaiah 66:15).

culture.title: Counted worthy
culture.text: Paul speaks of their suffering as evidence of "the righteous judgment of God."

2 Thessalonians 2.audience: Believers upset by rumours about the end would have heard calm instruction to stand fast and hold the traditions they were taught, with a prayer that God stablish them in every good word and work.

culture.title: Forged letters
culture.text: Letters written under someone else's name were known in the ancient world. Paul ends this letter with his own handwriting as a sign (2 Thessalonians 3:17).

culture.title: Sitting in the temple of God
culture.text: Antiochus IV set up a pagan altar in the temple in 167 BC, and in AD 40 the emperor Caligula ordered his statue placed in the Jerusalem temple, though it was never done.

2 Thessalonians 3.audience: Paul addresses some "which walk among you disorderly, working not at all" (2 Thessalonians 3:11) and signs the letter himself.

culture.title: If any would not work
culture.text: Most people worked with their hands. Some poorer citizens depended on wealthy patrons for food and money.

culture.title: The token in every epistle
culture.text: Letters were usually written by a scribe; a closing in the sender's own hand showed that it was genuine.

1 Timothy 1.audience: Timothy, left to face false teachers in a busy city, would have heard Paul remind him that the aim of the charge is love and that mercy reached even the chief of sinners.

culture.title: Fables and endless genealogies
culture.text: Some Jewish writings of the time retold and expanded the genealogies and stories of Genesis.

culture.title: Menstealers
culture.text: Kidnapping people to sell as slaves was punishable by death in the law (Exodus 21:16).

culture.title: Delivered unto Satan
culture.text: Paul uses the same phrase for putting someone out of the church in 1 Corinthians 5:5.

1 Timothy 2.audience: A church in a city full of pagan temples would have heard that prayer is to be made for all men, even kings, because one God and one mediator wants all to be saved.

culture.title: Lifting up holy hands
culture.text: Jews and Gentiles commonly prayed standing with hands raised.

culture.title: Broided hair, gold, pearls
culture.text: Elaborate braided hairstyles with gold and pearls were a mark of wealth among Roman women. Moral writers criticized such display.

1 Timothy 3.audience: Believers choosing leaders in a new church would have heard that the test is character, home life, and a good report from outsiders.

culture.title: The husband of one wife
culture.text: Roman society praised a woman who had been married only once (univira). The phrase has been read as forbidding polygamy, remarriage, or unfaithfulness.

culture.title: Given to hospitality
culture.text: Traveling believers depended on hosts, since inns had a poor reputation.

1 Timothy 4.audience: Paul warns of those "forbidding to marry, and commanding to abstain from meats" (1 Timothy 4:3) and encourages Timothy, who was young.

culture.title: Bodily exercise
culture.text: Greek cities had gymnasiums where young men trained in athletics as part of their education.

culture.title: Let no man despise thy youth
culture.text: ‘Youth’ could describe anyone up to about forty. Elders were expected to be older men.

culture.title: Laying on of hands
culture.text: The elders laid hands on Timothy, as Moses did to Joshua (Numbers 27:23).

1 Timothy 5.audience: Families and widows in the church, and its older men who led it, would have heard how God's household is to care for the helpless and treat its leaders fairly.

culture.title: Widows indeed
culture.text: Widows without family often had no means of support. The law commanded care for them (Deuteronomy 24:19–21).

culture.title: Threescore years old
culture.text: Sixty was a common age for being counted elderly.

culture.title: A little wine
culture.text: Water was often unsafe; wine was commonly used as a remedy for stomach complaints.

1 Timothy 6.audience: Paul warns those who teach for gain and charges "them that are rich in this world" (1 Timothy 6:17).

culture.title: Under the yoke
culture.text: Some Christian slaves had Christian masters.

culture.title: Contentment
culture.text: The word was a Stoic term for self-sufficiency. Job 1:21 says, "Naked came I out of my mother's womb."

culture.title: Before Pontius Pilate
culture.text: This is the only mention of Pilate in Paul's letters.

2 Timothy 1.audience: Timothy, who may have feared standing with a jailed teacher, would have heard that the Spirit given is one of power, love, and a sound mind, and that one friend was not ashamed.

culture.title: Lois and Eunice
culture.text: Timothy's mother was Jewish and his father Greek (Acts 16:1). Mothers often taught children the Scriptures at home (2 Timothy 3:15).

culture.title: Not ashamed of my chain
culture.text: Visiting a prisoner brought shame and risk, and friends had to bring food. Onesiphorus searched Rome to find Paul (2 Timothy 1:17).

culture.title: That which I have committed
culture.text: The Greek word means a deposit entrusted to someone for safekeeping.

2 Timothy 2.audience: Paul urges Timothy to endure hardship and to pass on what he learned "to faithful men" (2 Timothy 2:2).

culture.title: Soldier, athlete, farmer
culture.text: Roman soldiers were forbidden to take up civilian business. Athletes in the games swore to keep the rules of training and competition.

culture.title: Rightly dividing
culture.text: The Greek word means to cut straight, as in cutting a road or plowing a furrow.

culture.title: Vessels in a great house
culture.text: A wealthy household had vessels of gold and silver for honored use and of wood and clay for common tasks.

2 Timothy 3.audience: Paul warns of hard times in "the last days" and reminds Timothy that he has known the Scriptures from childhood (2 Timothy 3:15).

culture.title: Jannes and Jambres
culture.text: Jewish tradition named the Egyptian magicians who opposed Moses (Exodus 7:11) Jannes and Jambres.

culture.title: Creeping into houses
culture.text: Traveling teachers often sought support from wealthy households.

culture.title: Antioch, Iconium, Lystra
culture.text: These are the cities of Paul's first journey, near Timothy's home (Acts 13–14; 16:1).

2 Timothy 4.audience: Timothy and the church would have read the last words of a man facing the end, and learned that the Lord stood with him when everyone else left.

culture.title: Poured out
culture.text: A drink offering of wine was poured out on the altar (Numbers 28:7).

culture.title: The cloak and the parchments
culture.text: A cloak was a heavy outer garment; Roman prisons were cold. Parchments were writing sheets made from animal skin.

culture.title: Before winter
culture.text: Sea travel stopped for the winter months (Acts 27:9–12).

Titus 1.audience: Young churches in a place known for liars and loose living would have heard what kind of man to trust as a leader, and why deceivers must be stopped.

culture.title: Crete
culture.text: Crete is a large island south of Greece with many cities. It had a Jewish community (Acts 2:11).

culture.title: Cretians are always liars
culture.text: Paul quotes a poet from Crete, traditionally Epimenides. Greeks used ‘to Cretanize’ to mean ‘to lie.’

Titus 2.audience: Believers of every age, and servants in other people's houses, would have heard that quiet, steady lives made the gospel look good to outsiders.

culture.title: Not given to much wine
culture.text: Roman writers mocked older women who drank heavily.

culture.title: Not purloining
culture.text: Household slaves handled their masters' goods, and petty theft by slaves was a common complaint.

Titus 3.audience: Believers who were once as foolish as anyone would have heard that they were saved by mercy, not works, and were sent back into daily life to do good and be gentle with all.

culture.title: Nicopolis
culture.text: Nicopolis was a city on the west coast of Greece founded by Augustus to celebrate his victory at Actium in 31 BC.

culture.title: Zenas the lawyer
culture.text: Zenas may have been trained in Jewish law or Roman law; Paul does not say which.

Philemon 1.audience: Philemon, his house church, and Onesimus himself would have heard Paul ask a master to welcome a returning slave as a beloved brother, with Paul standing good for any debt.

culture.title: Onesimus departed
culture.text: Paul does not say why Onesimus left. Runaway slaves could be severely punished. A letter by Pliny the Younger asks a friend to forgive a freedman who had wronged him.

culture.title: Onesimus
culture.text: Onesimus means ‘useful’—a common slave name. Paul plays on it: "unprofitable" then, "profitable" now.

culture.title: Put that on mine account
culture.text: Paul writes an IOU in his own hand, as in a business document: "I Paul have written it with mine own hand, I will repay it."
